Load a vision model that runs on ONNX Runtime, without PyTorch

Source: R/onnx.R
onnxModel.Rd

The light way to embed images and texts: the Python side needs only onnxruntime, numpy, pillow and tokenizers (about 150 MB installed, against 0.8 GB to several GB for PyTorch, depending on the platform). The result is used exactly like a visionModel(): with embedImages(), embedTexts(), scoreImages(), suggestSpecies() and the rest. visionModel(backend = "onnx") calls this function.

Usage

onnxModel(
  name = "clip-vit-base-patch32",
  precision = c("fp32", "fp16", "int8"),
  textPrecision = precision,
  text = TRUE,
  cache = onnxCache(),
  python = NULL,
  threads = 0,
  fetch = NULL
)

Arguments

name

The model: a folder, a Hugging Face repository or a known name (see below).

precision

"fp32", "fp16" or "int8": which copy of the image encoder to use.

textPrecision

The same for the text encoder; by default as precision.

text

If FALSE, the text encoder is not downloaded (about 250 MB less at "fp32"). embedTexts() then fails; sniglet keys do not need it.

cache

Folder for downloaded models.

python

Optional path to the Python executable to use (passed to reticulate::use_python()).

threads

Number of CPU threads for ONNX Runtime; 0 lets it choose.

fetch

For tests: a function (url, dest) that downloads a file and returns TRUE, or FALSE if there is no such file.

Value

An object of class dimooseVisionModel, as visionModel() returns, with a files entry: the model's folder (dir), its image and text encoder files (image, text) and, for a model from the Hub, its repository (repo) and the web address of the image encoder (imageUrl).

Where models come from

name is one of

  • a folder on your computer that holds an ONNX model (also written "local-dir:<folder>"), in either layout described below;

  • a Hugging Face repository, "<organisation>/<model>" or "hf-hub:<organisation>/<model>". The files that are needed are downloaded once into onnxCache() and reused; nothing is downloaded when they are already there;

  • "clip-vit-base-patch32" (the default; CLIP ViT-B/32, the same weights as visionModel()) or "clip-vit-base-patch16": the ready-made exports Xenova/clip-vit-base-patch32 and Xenova/clip-vit-base-patch16 on the Hub;

  • "mobileclip-s0": Apple's MobileCLIP-S0 (Xenova/mobileclip_s0), a small model for phones. Its image encoder is 46 MB at "fp32" and 23 MB at "fp16". Its "int8" file is refused: its embeddings are wrong (measured: cosine 0.09 on average with the "fp32" ones);

  • "bioclip", "bioclip-2" or any other model you have converted with exportOnnxModel(). There is no official ONNX copy of BioCLIP on the Hub, so it has to be converted once on a computer with PyTorch; the converted folder can then be copied to computers without it.

Precision and size

Each encoder comes in up to three precisions. Measured on dimoose's 55 example photos against the PyTorch model (CLIP ViT-B/32 image encoder):

precisionimage encodercosine with PyTorch (lowest)
"fp32"352 MB1.0000
"fp16"176 MB1.0000
"int8", converted by exportOnnxModel()96 MB0.998
"int8", Xenova/clip-vit-base-patch32 (_quantized)89 MB0.81

"fp16" halves the download but runs up to three times slower on a CPU than "fp32". BioCLIP converted by exportOnnxModel() is 345, 173 and 89 MB, with cosines of 1.0000, 1.0000 and 0.998 (BioCLIP 2, a larger model, is about 1217, 609 and 310 MB); on the Montana example photos all three precisions name the same species. A key must be followed with the model and precision it was built with when the precision is "int8": its embeddings differ slightly from the others'. The ready-made "int8" file of Xenova/clip-vit-base-patch32 is a much rougher copy (0.89 on average), so onnxModel() warns when it is used; to get the close one, convert the model yourself with exportOnnxModel("ViT-B-32"). A model you have converted is used in place of the ready-made copy of the same name.

The patch tokens of an "int8" encoder (embedImages(tiles = 0)) are less faithful than its image embeddings: with BioCLIP the lowest cosine of a token with the "fp32" one was 0.86. Use tiles, or a higher precision, to find sniglets with patch tokens.

Layouts of a model folder

dimoose's own layout, written by exportOnnxModel(): dimoose_onnx.json (architecture, image size, preprocessing constants, file names), image_encoder.onnx, text_encoder.onnx, their _fp16 and _int8 copies, and tokenizer.json. Its image encoder also returns the model's patch tokens, so embedImages(tiles = 0) works.

The transformers.js layout of ready-made exports on the Hub: config.json, preprocessor_config.json, tokenizer.json, onnx/vision_model[_fp16|_quantized].onnx and onnx/text_model[_fp16|_quantized].onnx. These give one embedding per image and no patch tokens: tiles (the default of embedImages()) work, tiles = 0 does not.

When something goes wrong

  • Could not download ...: the model is fetched from huggingface.co the first time only. Files that arrived are kept, so calling again continues where it stopped. A computer that cannot reach the Hub can be given the model's folder, copied from onnxCache() on one that can, as name.

  • ... is not a readable ONNX model: a model file is damaged, usually a download or copy that stopped early. Delete the file named in the message and load the model again; a file from the Hub is fetched afresh.

  • Could not load dimoose's ONNX code: the Python in use lacks onnxruntime or tokenizers. The message gives the reticulate::py_install() call that installs them.

See also

exportOnnxModel() to convert a model, exportBrowserModel() to use one in a web page, saveEmbeddings() to need no Python at all.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
model <- onnxModel()                              # CLIP ViT-B/32, downloaded once
model <- onnxModel(precision = "fp16")            # half the download
images <- imageSet(system.file("extdata", "pics", package = "dimoose"))
emb <- embedImages(model, images)

exportOnnxModel("bioclip")                        # once, needs PyTorch
model <- onnxModel("bioclip")                     # afterwards, without it
} # }
